Odontesthes nigricans, commonly known as the silverside, is a marine teleost of the family Atherinopsidae that inhabits the coastal waters of southern South America. Field surveys and laboratory growth studies have established that this species attains a maximum standard length of 21.6 centimeters [Li = 21.6 centimeters], although some ichthyological records report a total length of 18 centimeters [Li = 18 centimeters] for fully grown individuals captured in trawl samples. This ultimate body size places Odontesthes nigricans among the smaller members of its genus, with the largest documented specimens rarely exceeding the 21.6 centimeter [Li = 21.6 centimeter] mark. The species exhibits a moderately fast growth trajectory during its first two years of life, after which the rate of length increase decelerates markedly as individuals approach their asymptotic size. Sexual differentiation becomes externally apparent when the fish reach a standard length of approximately 12 centimeters, which corresponds to the onset of gonadal development and the progression toward functional maturity.

The transition to reproductive competence in Odontesthes nigricans is closely tied to both body size and somatic mass accumulation. Individuals attain puberty, defined by the initiation of gametogenesis and the first visible differentiation of the gonads, once they have reached a total length of 12 centimeters [Lp = 12 centimeters]. This length-based threshold corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 10.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 10.7 grams], as estimated from the length–mass relationship derived for this species. The mass gain from the larval stage through to the onset of puberty is substantial, reflecting the accumulation of structural tissues and the development of reproductive organs. Field-collected specimens at the point of sexual maturation consistently exhibit this body mass, which represents a critical energetic milestone. Individuals below this weight are rarely found to possess active gonadal tissue, indicating that a minimum somatic investment is required before the onset of reproductive activity. This pattern aligns with the general life-history strategy of iteroparous marine fishes in temperate environments.

The reproductive output of Odontesthes nigricans has been quantified through a combination of fecundity assessments and spawning frequency observations conducted under controlled thermal conditions. When maintained at a stable water temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], captive females produce an average of 4,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 4,000 eggs per spawning event], with a clutch frequency of approximately one spawning event per year [F_R_i = approximately one spawning event per year]. This high fecundity is characteristic of small-bodied atherinopsids that rely on batch spawning to maximize annual reproductive output. The corresponding daily egg production rate, derived from the product of clutch size and frequency, yields a substantial total over the extended spawning season. The 12 °C [T = 12 °C] thermal regime used in these experiments mirrors the typical austral spring temperatures encountered in the species' native range, ensuring that the measured reproductive rates reflect ecologically relevant conditions. Comparisons with the congener Odontesthes regia suggest that the fecundity of Odontesthes nigricans scales broadly with body size.

Early life stages of Odontesthes nigricans exhibit pronounced dependency on maternally provisioned yolk reserves, which sustain the developing embryo and the yolk-sac larva through the critical period before the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth, measured immediately following eclosion, is approximately 0.0056 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0056 grams], reflecting the modest size of the incubating egg and the limited yolk volume available for early development. This neonatal mass, derived from an egg diameter range of 1.8 to 2.5 millimeters typical of the genus, positions the newly emerged larva as a small, initially lecithotrophic propagule. The yolk-sac larva absorbs its endogenous nutrient store over the first several days post-hatching, a period during which the mouth gapes opens and retinal differentiation enables prey detection. The subsequent transition to first feeding marks a critical nutritional bottleneck, as the larva must successfully capture planktonic prey to avoid starvation. Data from laboratory rearing experiments indicate that mortality is highest during this brief window of nutritional vulnerability.

Adult Odontesthes nigricans reach a maximum wet weight of 62.7 grams [Wwi = 62.7 grams] under optimal growing conditions, a value that corresponds closely with the asymptotic standard length observed in the population. This ultimate wet weight is achieved through a prolonged period of somatic growth that extends over the majority of the species' lifespan, with the most rapid mass gain occurring prior to the attainment of sexual maturity. The maximum lifespan for the species, documented under stable captive conditions at a controlled temperature of 12 °C [T = 12 °C], is 2,555 days [am = 2,555 days], which represents approximately seven years [am = approximately seven years] of sustained physiological function. This longevity is relatively modest compared to larger-bodied marine fishes but is consistent with the life-history expectations for a small, fast-growing teleost occupying a temperate coastal niche. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in reproductive output and a reduction in somatic condition, with most natural mortality events recorded from the sixth year onward. Long-term field mark-recapture programs have corroborated the captive lifespan estimate, with very few free-living individuals exceeding the seven-year mark.
